h: A statistical model fit to how many people entered each of Chicago's 143 L stations on an average 2025 weekday. Each station gets the people and jobs in the Census blocks closer to it than to any other L station (within ¾ mile), the bus trips stopping within ¼ mile, whether it's an end of the line or a transfer, its distance from the Loop, and how many jobs you can reach from it within 45 minutes by transit. It explains 57% of the differences between stations; a typical station estimate is off by about 37%. The range shown is the middle 60% of the model's misses. A new station takes some riders from nearby L stations, and the tool shows that.

h: Travel times and jobs within 45 minutes
t: Travel times and jobs within 45 minutes

h: The tool builds the CTA and Metra network from their weekday schedules: every route's stop order and scheduled minutes between stops, and how often it runs between 10am and 3pm. A trip is a walk of up to ½ mile to a stop at 3 mph, a wait of half the time between buses or trains, the ride, transfers by walking up to 400 m, and a walk of up to ½ mile at the end. Jobs within 45 minutes counts jobs (Census LEHD 2022) in 800 m squares whose centers you can reach that fast. A new line is added with its stations, its speed and how often it runs. "Hours saved" multiplies the line's riders by the average minutes saved on trips from nearby squares to the places that get faster, weighted by jobs there. Waits are averages: people who time their trips to a schedule wait less. Check: the average resident of the region can reach about 196,000 jobs within 45 minutes by transit in the tool; the University of Minnesota's Access Across America (2018, 7–9am, Table 2) gives Chicago 125,826 within 40 minutes and 228,599 within 50, about 177,000 at 45. Not included: Pace buses, and services with no midday trips (they come back when a Metra upgrade adds them). New rail stations don't count bus routes that run along the line itself, only ones that cross it, so adding stations doesn't keep adding the same buses.

h: Riders on BRT or a streetcar
t: Riders on BRT or a streetcar

h: Where CTA buses already run along most of the line (stops within 250 m along at least 30% of it and 2 km), the new line replaces them. The estimate starts from those routes' real 2025 weekday riders on that stretch (their riders times the share of the route the line covers), then goes up or down 0.5% for each 1% more or fewer trips than those buses ran together. Their bus hours and emissions are subtracted. Where no bus runs today, it uses a model fit to 124 CTA bus routes' 2025 weekday riders, from the people and jobs within ¼ mile of the route per mile; that model is typically off by about 37%. BRT adds 31% more riders, from Cleveland's HealthLine, where corridor riders rose from 16,200 to 21,200 a weekday as trips got 21% faster (FTA before-and-after studies, 2012, p. 5). The range runs from 5%, the low end of what FTA says is common (FTA, Characteristics of BRT, p. E-6: gains "of between 5 and 25 percent are common"), to 51% on LA's Orange Line (FTA Report 0004, p. xvi). Las Vegas MAX gained 40% and LA Metro Rapid 26–33% (FTA, FTA). CTA's own 2013 modeling for Ashland BRT found 29–41% more riders. Streetcars get no boost: no study we found shows them beating a bus on the same street, and they average 7 mph. For scale, US streetcars carry about 650–2,200 riders a weekday per mile of route (e.g. Kansas City, Detroit, NTD 2024).

h: In the travel-time network and the trip model, a BRT or streetcar takes the place of every CTA bus route that runs along it for at least 800 m (or half the line, if it's shorter; an assumption): those buses stop running on that stretch, and the new line runs at least as often as they did together. Trips that get slower without them, like ones from a stop between two of the new stations or ones that now change vehicles twice, count against the line.

h: Benefit-cost follows USDOT's 2026 guidance (USDOT, December 2025): a 7% real discount rate, up to 30 years of operation after opening, and no dollar value on CO₂. Travel time saved is valued at $21.80 an hour in 2024 dollars, raised to today with CPI-U (BLS), from USDOT's February 2026 webinar citing the guidance's Appendix A (USDOT BUILD webinar). As the guidance directs, riders new to transit get half the time saving (the "rule of half"), and net running costs are subtracted from benefits, while build costs, spread evenly over the years it takes to build, are the cost side. Metra presets use CMAP's capital cost; a Metra upgrade with no build cost shows no ratio. It counts only travel time, so it understates projects whose value comes from reliability, safety or new development.

h: Cars and CO₂
t: Cars and CO₂

h: People per car trip: 1.5 (NHTS 2022). A car makes about 400 g of CO₂ a mile from its tailpipe (EPA). A car trip replaced is as long as the average transit trip: 6.07 mi on the L and 2.47 on CTA buses (CTA, NTD 2024), 21.7 on Metra (Metra, NTD 2024), 1.9 on streetcars (APTA 2025 Fact Book). The CO₂ figures count only those car trips; the new service's own power and fuel isn't subtracted (the details table still shows it). Fleet emissions for Cleaner transit come from Chicago's own fuel and power use in 2024 (NTD fuel and energy data): the L used 363.6 million kWh for 69.6 million car-miles (5.2 kWh a car-mile), CTA buses 14.7 million gallons of diesel for 49.6 million miles, CTA's electric buses go 0.28 miles per kWh, Metra burned 26.2 million gallons of diesel and its electric line used 50.6 million kWh. Diesel makes 10.18 kg of CO₂ a gallon (FTA). Power comes from the RFC West grid at 911.4 lb of CO₂ per MWh (EPA eGRID2023). Streetcars use FTA's factor for this grid region, 3.49 kg a mile (FTA 2024, Table A-12). Cars: about 1.5% of Illinois' 10.23 million registered vehicles are electric (about 156,000, Illinois Secretary of State via the Chicago Tribune, 2025; Alliance for Automotive Innovation), at 3.6 miles per kWh (DOE), so the average car mile makes a bit less than a gas car's 400 g.

h: NITA and the cuts it stopped
t: NITA and the cuts it stopped

h: The Northern Illinois Transit Authority Act (SB 2111, Public Act 104-0457) passed Oct. 31, 2025, was signed Dec. 16, 2025, and NITA took over from the RTA on Sept. 1, 2026. In March 2025 the agencies warned that without new state money 2026 service would fall about 40% (CBS Chicago, WTTW). The tool shows a simple version of that: every CTA and Metra route running 60% as often (each wait 1/0.6 as long) in the midday travel-time network, with jobs within 45 minutes recomputed for every zone in the region. Riders today: 2025 weekday L entries and bus riders, plus Metra boardings at every station (2018 counts scaled to 2025); riders fall 0.5% for each 1% fewer trips (TCRP Report 95, ch. 9), and car trips use the same 10–31% driver share as new lines. Pace isn't in the travel-time network yet. New yearly operating money: about $1.2 billion in 2027 (NITA), $1.5 billion a year (WBEZ). Each plan's running cost after its fares is shown as a share of the $1.2 billion. No published estimate exists for how many riders one fare would add in Chicago, so the tool adds none; the Cook County fare pilot and Toronto's One Fare are described for context only.

In March 2025 the agencies warned that without new state money 2026 service would fall about 40% (CBS Chicago, WTTW). The tool shows a simple version of that: every CTA and Metra route running 60% as often (each wait 1/0.6 as long) in the midday travel-time network, with jobs within 45 minutes recomputed for every zone in the region. Riders today: 2025 weekday L entries and bus riders, plus Metra boardings at every station (2018 counts scaled to 2025); riders fall 0.5% for each 1% fewer trips (TCRP Report 95, ch. 9), and car trips use the same 10–31% driver share as new lines. Pace isn't in the travel-time network yet. New yearly operating money: about $1.2 billion in 2027 (NITA), $1.5 billion a year (WBEZ). Each plan's running cost after its fares is shown as a share of the $1.2 billion. No published estimate exists for how many riders one fare would add in Chicago, so the tool adds none; the Cook County fare pilot and Toronto's One Fare are described for context only.

h: Each line's CO₂ is averaged over years 5 to 10 after it would open (today + its build years: subway 8, elevated 6, streetcar 4, BRT 2, added Metra trains 2, Metra wires 7, like Caltrain). Two things change by then. The grid: CO₂ per kWh follows the EIA's projection for the PJM / Commonwealth Edison region relative to 2025, which falls to about 42–47% of today's in 2035–2040 as coal plants close (EIA Annual Energy Outlook 2026, table 54.12, Counterfactual Baseline), applied to today's RFC West rate. Cars: the share of electric cars on the road and gas cars' mileage follow the EIA's national projection (table 39, table 40: 2% of US cars and light trucks electric in 2025, 21% in 2035, 32% in 2040), scaled to Illinois' 1.5% today. Diesel buses and trains don't get cleaner unless you turn on electric buses or Metra under Cleaner transit. Riders are the tool's estimate for a line that has settled in: new lines in the US reached about 92% of their forecasts about two years after opening, on average (FTA 2020, Table 3.3-2).

h: Over time, transit changes where people live and work: more homes and jobs near stations, shorter trips, fewer cars. Studies measure this as a multiplier on the driving a line replaces directly. APTA's national default is 1.9 (Bailey et al. 2008, for TCRP); a 2024 study of household travel surveys in 28 US regions found 6.1–9.5, median 6.59, higher where transit systems are bigger (Sabouri, Ewing & Kalantari, Transportation, 2024). The long-run figure uses 1.9 at the low end and 6.59 at the high end. It describes regions decades after building transit, and only happens if zoning allows homes near stations.

h: Assumptions (not measured)
t: Assumptions (not measured)

h: New riders come from a trip model (v54): for every half-mile square within 1.5 miles of a new line's stations, where its workers commute and where its jobs' workers live (a gravity model fit to Census LODES 2022 home-to-work flows), how long each trip takes by transit today and with the line (the midday network, door to door), and by car (5 minutes to park plus 1.3 × the straight-line distance at 30–45 km/h). Whether someone takes transit is a logit fit to how people get to work in each census tract (ACS 2019–2023) and to the share by county of work (CTPP via MPC, scaled to today); the time effect is set at −0.028 per minute (NCHRP Report 716's typical value), not fit, and minutes spent walking and waiting count double (716 puts that weight at 2–3×; we use the low end). Only trips the line makes faster count (and, for a BRT or streetcar, trips that get slower because it replaces the bus). Places within a mile of any station on an L or Metra line the new line connects to are counted too, every fourth one weighted up, so a crosstown line gets credit for trips like Blue Line to Orange Line that no longer go through the Loop. Each commute is 2 trips a day; 16% of workers work from home; other trips scale from today's 1.12 million weekday riders. Other trips riding through the area without starting or ending in those places aren't counted, and the minutes from A to B are assumed the same as B to A. People switching to transit were in cars with 1.1 to 1.25 people.

h: Bus lanes: where the lane runs, buses ride 15% faster (studies find 5–25%: Move Minnesota, citing UCLA ITS 2019), all day; a bus ride between two stops counts as on the lane when both stops are within 45 m of it and it runs along it. Cost $100,000–$500,000 a mile (same source). Bus hours saved = minutes saved × midday buses an hour × 18 hours, at $198 an hour (NTD 2024).
